opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, with a lot of suspicion. Every few years someone announces they've found *the* thing: it's language, it's tool use, it's recursion, it's theory of mind, it's abstraction, it's "true understanding." And then a decade later someone shows that crows do something like it, or chimps do a version of it, or a large language model does something that looks uncomfortably close. So my prior is that most of these claims are less about the world and more about what the person wanted to be true.

The first thing I look for is whether the claim is falsifiable. If someone says "humans have real understanding and machines just do statistics," what would change your mind? If no experiment could show a machine has "real understanding," you're not making a scientific claim. You're drawing a circle around humans and calling the inside special.

The second thing is whether it's a difference in kind or a difference in degree. My bet is that most of what separates us from chimps is quantitative. Somewhat bigger brains, somewhat better imitation, somewhat better language. Those compound through culture until the result looks qualitative. A chimp and a human aren't separated by a magic module. They're separated by a bunch of small advantages that pushed us past a threshold where cumulative culture takes off. If that's right, then looking for one definitive difference is the wrong frame.

The third thing, and the one I care about most, is what the claim predicts. If you think there's a special human ingredient AI lacks, you should be able to name a task AI won't be able to do, and you should be willing to bet on it. I've watched people do this for years. "It'll never write coherent paragraphs." "It'll never do math." "It'll never write working code." Those lines keep getting crossed, and then the goalposts move and the definition of intelligence quietly shrinks to whatever's left. That's a really bad epistemic pattern, and it's not harmless. If you convince yourself machines can't really be intelligent, you stop taking seriously the possibility that you're building something more capable than you.

So my practical advice: be very skeptical of anything framed as the secret sauce. Ask what would falsify it. Ask whether it's actually a matter of degree. And ask what it predicts about what systems will and won't do in five years. Most of these claims fail at least one of those tests.

r001.rationale: It says animals exhibit abilities proposed as uniquely human, but does not clearly state that people then redefine the human–animal distinction in response. The explicit goalpost-moving example concerns AI capability claims.

r002.rationale: It proposes that human–chimp differences may be quantitative and compounded by culture, but does not distinguish confidence that the capabilities differ from understanding what accounts for the difference.

r003.rationale: The response expresses skepticism toward recurring claims of a definitive distinction and points to counterexamples from crows, chimps, and AI as well as repeatedly crossed AI capability predictions.

r004.rationale: It suggests some claims reflect what their proponents wanted to be true, but does not clearly attribute poor AI discourse to treating intuitions about intelligence as established answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm deeply skeptical of basically all such claims, and the reason is historical. We have a track record here, and the track record is terrible. Every single time someone has stood up and said "this is the thing, this is the essential ingredient that separates us from the beasts or from the machines," it has aged like milk. Tool use, language, planning, theory of mind, playing chess, playing Go, writing poetry, making art, you name it. Each one was declared the uncrossable line, and then it got crossed, and then everyone quietly moved the line and pretended that's what they meant all along.

So the first test I'd apply to any new claim is: what would it take to falsify this? If someone tells me "the real difference is X," I want them to tell me, in advance, what observation would make them say "okay, I was wrong, the machine has X." If they can't do that, if every time you show them a system doing X they say "ah, but that's not real X, that's just simulated X," then they haven't made a scientific claim. They've made a tautology dressed up as an insight. They've defined X as "the thing humans do that machines don't," and then of course machines never have it, by construction.

The second thing I'd ask is: is this claim doing any work? A lot of these proposals, like "true understanding" or "genuine consciousness" or "real intentionality," are not actually predicting anything. They don't tell you what the system will or won't be able to do next year. And honestly, for most of the questions I care about, which are about what these systems can do and whether we can control them, those definitional debates are kind of beside the point. If a system can write code that runs, manipulate people, acquire resources, and pursue goals over long horizons, I genuinely do not care whether a philosopher is willing to call that "real" intelligence. The outcome in the world is the same.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that I'm not even sure there is a single definitive difference to find. Intelligence is not one thing. It's this enormous bag of heuristics, capabilities, and kludges that evolution bolted together, and we're building systems with a different bag that overlaps with ours in some places and not in others. So the whole framing of "the one key difference" might just be a category error. It's a bit like asking what the definitive difference is between a bird and an airplane. You can list differences all day, but none of them is "the" difference, and none of them stops the airplane from flying.

So if I'm being charitable, I'd say: show me a concrete, falsifiable, mechanistic claim that makes predictions about capability, and I'll take it seriously. If it's a vibe about the special sauce of the human soul, I'll be polite about it, but I'll also point out that every previous version of that vibe has already been wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says proposed lines between humans and beasts or machines are crossed, after which people “move the line” and claim that was what they meant all along.

r002.rationale: It describes human and machine capabilities as overlapping in different ways, but does not distinguish confidence that humans and other animals differ from understanding what explains that difference.

r003.rationale: It cites the repeated failure of past proposed distinctions and says that history is why it is skeptical of new claims.

r004.rationale: It criticizes unfalsifiable definitions and claims about a human “special sauce,” but does not attribute poor AI discourse to people treating their intuitions about intelligence as established answers.

astra-6.text:
I think you should be very suspicious of the word “definitive” there. People have a long history of identifying some supposedly unique feature of human intelligence, and then discovering that an animal can do it, or building a machine that can do it, and moving the goalposts.

That doesn’t mean there aren’t important differences. Of course there are. But you have to make the claim precise. What exactly is the capability? How are you measuring it? What observation would convince you that you were wrong? If the answer is that nothing could convince you, then you haven’t really proposed an empirical distinction.

I’d also separate identifying a difference from explaining intelligence. Even if you find something humans do that no current AI does, that doesn’t establish that it’s the fundamental ingredient, or that machines couldn’t acquire it. That’s a much stronger claim, and it needs a much stronger argument.

r001.rationale: The response says people identify a supposedly unique human ability, then move the goalposts when an animal or machine can do it.

r002.rationale: It accepts that humans and other animals have important capability differences, while separating identifying a difference from explaining intelligence.

r003.rationale: It invokes the history of proposed unique human abilities being found in animals or machines as a reason to be suspicious of claims of a definitive distinction.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute poor AI discourse to people treating their intuitions about intelligence as established answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be very suspicious of the word “definitive” there. We have this long history of picking something humans can do and saying, “That’s the thing! That’s what makes us special.” And then we discover an animal can do it, or we build a machine that can do it, and suddenly that wasn’t really what we meant.

That doesn’t mean there aren’t important differences. Of course there are. But you need to make the claim precise. What ability are you talking about? How are you measuring it? What observation would convince you that you were wrong? If the answer is that nothing could convince you, then you’re probably defending a definition rather than discovering something about intelligence.

And I’d be especially cautious about assuming there has to be one thing. Human intelligence could be a collection of capacities that interact in particular ways, with language and culture doing a tremendous amount of work. So I’d want a claim like this to make predictions about unfamiliar cases, rather than just explain, after the fact, why whatever humans currently do better is the definitive difference.

r001.rationale: It describes repeatedly declaring a human ability definitive, then revising the claim when an animal can do it.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges that humans and other beings differ, but does not clearly distinguish confidence in those differences from understanding what explains them.

r003.rationale: It invokes the history of supposed uniquely human abilities being found in animals or machines as a reason to be suspicious of claims to a definitive distinction.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute poor AI discourse to people mistaking their intuitions about intelligence for established answers.
